paragraphs: Pronouns.
Or how to write and speak without using the same nouns over and over again.
Pronouns substitute for nouns.
Pronoun allow writers to be efficient.
They let writers play with the sound and rhythm of a sentence.
They create variety by helping writers avoid repeating the same noun many times in a paragraph.
English has seventy-four pronouns.
These pronouns work in 8 different ways. We call these pronouns: personal, demonstrative, indefinite, interrogative, reciprocal, intensive, reflexive, and relative.
You may recognize these pronouns. You might already know how to use them.
Don’t worry. We’re not asking you to remember the “rules of grammar” for a quiz.
This presentation is to serve as a review and a reference.
You learn to use pronouns correctly by practicing reading, listening, and writing. Reading out loud is also very helpful.
Personal pronouns refer to people. They are commonly used, but are sometimes complicated.
Like verbs, personal pronouns take on several forms depending on their use.
To understand and correctly use personal pronouns, consider four simple things:

(4) gender (male/female)
*I/me = 1st person.  You = 2nd person.
He/she/it = 3rd person singular.  They/them = 3rd person plural.
Like nouns, personal pronouns can be a subject or an object. But unlike nouns, personal pronouns change depending on which function they perform. This is what we mean by “case.”
There are three kinds (cases) of personal pronouns. These are:
1. Subject
2. Object
3. Possessive
However, pronouns can also be adjectives, and these also have a “case.”

The term person identifies the relationship between the subject or object and the speaker or listener in the sentence. There are three “persons.”
These are first person (I), second person (you), and third person (he, she, or it).
But subjects and objects can also be singular or plural. This is what we mean when we talk about a pronoun’s number.

English also distinguishes between male and female (gender). This is easy. We have the pronoun couplets he / she and his / hers.
Gender only applies to the third person singular form. Third person plural is always gender neutral (they, them, theirs).
Demonstrative pronouns are easy. They point out something that we already know.
Demonstrative pronouns include this, that, these, and those.
We have very few problems with these pronouns. The only real problem is that/which confusion.
There is an easy way to decide whether to use that or which. Both “that” and “which” introduce a clause. A clause is a short group of words.
If the clause adds essential information to the sentence, it is called a restrictive clause and must use “that.”
If the clause does not contain essential information, it is a non-restrictive clause and must use “which.”
For example (courtesy of Purdue OWL):
The science fair, which lasted all day, ended with an awards ceremony.
The clause is non-restrictive. The most important information in the sentence is that the science fair ended with an awards ceremony.
For example (courtesy of Purdue OWL):
The police asked for every detail that would help identify the missing girl.
The clause is restrictive. The most important information in the sentence is NOT that the police asked for details, but rather, that the details were specific – they would identify the missing girl!
One final hint may help you. In most cases, non-restrictive clauses are set aside with commas. Restrictive clauses are less likely to be marked by punctuation.
Indefinite pronouns are less specific than demonstrative pronouns. They replace a noun without identifying the noun.
Indefinite pronouns may be singular, plural, or (in some cases) either.
Indefinite pronouns include:
Singular
another, anybody, anyone, anything, each, either, everybody, everyone, everything, little, much, neither, nobody, no one, nothing, one, other, somebody, someone, something
Plural
both, few, many, others, several
Singular or Plural
all, any, more, most, none, some
Examples of indefinite pronouns:
Singular: “Everybody knows something, but nobody knows everything.”
Plural: “Many enrolled for classes this fall.”
Singular or plural (singular):
“The furniture is antique. Most is in good condition.”
Singular or plural (plural):
“The menu boasts many exotic foods. All are delicious.”
Interrogative pronouns introduce questions. There are eleven interrogative pronouns.
They include who, whom, whose, what, which, whoever, whomever, whenever, whichever, whatever, and however.
Interrogative pronouns are not complicated, but in putting this lesson together we asked, if who and what are recognized as pronouns, then why aren’t when, where, how, and why included in that list?
In short, how, when, where, and why act like pronouns. They can substitute for a noun or noun phrase or, sometimes, an entire clause.
For example, take the sentence, “He quit his job because he got a better offer.”
Now consider the question, “Why did he quit his job?”
The original sentence is a compound sentence – two simple sentences connected by a conjunction.
“Why” is the interrogative substitute for the answer, which is the entire simple sentence, “He got a better offer.”
For this reason, why might not be considered a proper pronoun, but it still acts like one.
You won’t need to know this for an exam. The point is to illustrate the ways that language and grammar can be complicated.
One word can serve more than one role in English.
Relative pronouns function much like interrogative pronouns. A relative pronoun connects a subordinate clause to a noun that precedes it in a sentence.
Relative pronouns include: who, whom, whose, whoever, whomever, which, whichever, that, what, whatever.
For example:
“The man who wrote this book is a genius.”
“I can take the bus or bike, whichever is easiest.”
“The best essay, which I will choose, earns the writer a scholarship.
Reflexive pronouns end with -self. They include: myself, yourself, himself, herself, itself, oneself, ourselves, themselves, and yourselves.
Reflective pronouns point back to the subject of the sentence.
Examples:
She bought herself a new dress and a pair of shoes.
They wanted to kick themselves for losing the game.
Intensive pronouns are very similar to reflexive pronouns. They intensify (or call attention to) the nouns they represent. They are sometimes called “emphatic pronouns.”
They include: myself, yourself, himself, herself, itself, oneself, ourselves, themselves, and yourselves.
Examples:
“She, herself, made the dumplings.”
“You, yourselves, have to find the answers.”
“I, myself, will speak to the authorities.”
Note that reflexive and intensive pronouns (like personal pronouns) are sensitive to person and gender.
Reciprical pronouns show a mutual relationship. There are only two of them.
These are “one another” and “each other.”
Example: “My wife and I love each other.”
As we mentioned at the beginning of this presentation, people sometimes confuse pronouns and adjectives. Words such as “many” can be either.
For example, consider the following sentences:
“Many are called, but few are chosen.”
“Many men wish to become monks.”
In the first, many is a pronoun substituting for a noun.
In the second, many is an adjective describing men.
And consider the following sentences:
“Do you have any coffee?”
“No, I haven’t any.”
In the first, any is an adjective describing coffee.
In the second, any is a pronoun substituting for the noun, coffee.
Once again, we emphasize that this information is not for a quiz. This lesson is a reference to help your writing.
Choose your words carefully, thoughtfully. If you are not certain, review the information or ask for help.
Keeping your sentences short, and using SVO word order will help you to see the relationships between the words you choose.
Simplicity is the key to precise writing.
Eliminating unnecessary words avoids problems. Consider the following sentence:
A relative pronoun connects a subordinate clause to a noun that precedes it in a sentence. (16 words)
Relative pronouns connect subordinate clauses to nouns preceding them. (9 words)
In the revision, we see that the pronoun is not necessary.
So keep this in mind as you write and revise!
Writing hint #1:
We suggest that you use the noun BEFORE you use the pronoun. Use nouns in the first sentence of your paragraph.
You may know to whom you refer, but your reader won’t know. He or she will only see what you put on the page.
Writing hint #2:
Be careful when you have a sentence with more than one noun. If you use a pronoun in the following sentence, it must be very clear to which noun you refer. When in doubt, repeat the noun!
We look forward to reading your work!
